prompt:
A delivery van of mass 2100 kg is travelling along a straight level road at 15.0 m s^-1.
(a) Calculate the kinetic energy of the van. [1]
(b) The driver applies the brakes, providing a constant retarding force of 5200 N until the van stops. Calculate the minimum braking distance. [2]
(c) The van now travels at an initial speed of 30.0 m s^-1. Without carrying out a full numerical calculation, explain why the braking distance increases by a factor of 4. [1]

mark_scheme.criterion: Uses work-energy theorem W = F * s = E_k, so s = E_k / F = 236 250 / 5200 (or uses v^2 = u^2 + 2as with a = -F/m).
Calculates minimum braking distance s = 45.4 m (accept 45 m).

Explains that kinetic energy is proportional to the square of speed (E_k proportional to v^2) and retarding force is constant, so doubling speed quadruples the kinetic energy to be dissipated, quadrupling braking distance.

hints: In part (b), equate work done by braking force to initial kinetic energy: F * s = E_k.
In part (c), state the relationship between braking distance and initial speed when retarding force is constant.
solution:
(a) E_k = (1/2)mv^2 = 0.5 * 2100 kg * (15.0 m s^-1)^2 = 1050 * 225 = 236 250 J = 2.36 * 10^5 J (or 236 kJ).
(b) Work done by braking force W = F * s = E_k.
s = E_k / F = 236 250 J / 5200 N = 45.43 m = 45.4 m.
(c) Braking distance is directly proportional to initial kinetic energy (s = E_k / F) for a constant braking force. Because kinetic energy is proportional to the square of speed (E_k proportional to v^2), doubling the speed from 15.0 m s^-1 to 30.0 m s^-1 increases the kinetic energy by a factor of 2^2 = 4. Therefore, four times as much work must be done, resulting in four times the braking distance.
teacher_walkthrough: Part (b): Equate braking work to kinetic energy: Fs = E_k. s = 236 250 / 5200 = 45.4 m. Award C1, A1.
Part (c): Award B1 for explaining s proportional to v^2 via E_k proportional to v^2 and constant F.
Reinforce the road-safety implication of the quadratic speed dependence.
